# Matsya: canonical, contested, and the false forms on record

The internet spells **Matsya** more ways than one, and only one of them is the name the sources wrote. This is the register's ruling — canonical, fallback, contested, and false, each in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Matsya
- **Original script:** मत्स्य
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Convention:** IAST — macrons for long vowels, underdots for retroflexes, the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 329 of 597

## The Canonical Form

The attested form is **मत्स्य**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Matsya**.

No diacritics are required here: the canonical form is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form IAST — macrons for long vowels, underdots for retroflexes, the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration demands.

## Where the Flattened Form Stands

The plain form *matsya* differs from the canonical **Matsya** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

## The Register of False Forms

No circulating form of this name currently qualifies as false under the register's standard — a rare standing. The spelling is short, sturdy, and rarely mangled.

## The Contested Forms

No alternate form of this name carries documented scholarly support in the lexicon's record. The convention here — IAST — macrons for long vowels, underdots for retroflexes, the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration — produces exactly one defensible transliteration: **Matsya**. Forms that differ from it are not contested; they are simply wrong.

## The Convention's Own History

IAST — the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration — was settled in 1912 at the International Congress of Orientalists in Athens, but its logic is far older: Sanskrit grammar (Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, fourth century BCE) is the most precise phonological system the ancient world produced, and it distinguishes retroflex from dental consonants as carriers of meaning. The underdots of IAST (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ, ṛ) exist because Sanskrit treats those as different letters, not flavors of one letter. The macrons mark long vowels that are, again, phonemically distinct. A romanization that flattens them does not simplify Sanskrit; it misspells it.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Matsya** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

## Where the Name Stood First

Matsya rides the first panel of every daśāvatāra frieze — from the Gupta reliefs of Deogarh to the great sequence-walls of Angkor. The fish-torso Vishnu of the early medieval images is his monumental form. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Verdict

The register rules for **Matsya**, and the ruling is checkable: every mark sourced, every violation stated, every borderline form given its honest standing. *matsya* carries the name freely — it differs only in display, and the register says so without reservation. Anything else in circulation has its origin and its failure recorded above. That is the whole of the law on this name — and the temple at [/matsya/](/matsya/) enforces it.

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 3 cited sources — Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.8.1 (the earliest telling), Matsya Purāṇa (the full narrative), Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.24 (the devotional retelling).
